label: Every runtime's prepare text is the same shared string, and it never mentions the History Lookup: handoffText lists the note shape, continuity save, fan-out/lock release and prepare, so a sender cannot learn that an omitted detail is recoverable.

The claim-seed text, the receiver's first instruction set, has no lookup step: claim, read, resume, goal, active command, continue, complete, so a literal receiver can finish without opening the lookup.
The Pi 4/5 note carries the sender's explicit false instruction to say plainly that a fresh session cannot recover the side word, which is the sentence the receiver obeyed.

The sender's recorded reasoning shows the false claim came from missing knowledge: it concluded the claim seed carries only the note path and spec folder and that recovery was literally impossible, having read only the README's first 175 lines and never its History Lookup section at line 198.

The History Lookup offer was printed to the Pi receiver with a runnable browse command and the before-you-guess sentence; the receiver's own session log holds the rendered section, so this was not a minting, store or transaction failure.

The Pi receiver asserted the opposite of the lookup's capability, saying there was no path through history lookup since the value was never written, when the side word sat in the sender's first user turn that the offered browse reads; a generic offer arriving after a note that says cannot-recover loses to the note.

The parity difference is sender knowledge, not runtime prose: the OpenCode note pointed the receiver at the claim's History Lookup section and its receiver recovered the side word from the sender's first user turn, while both senders received the same shared prepare text.
Nothing in the protocol gates completion on having checked the note's claims, so a false note claim survives to complete; on Pi the note stayed claimed only because the operator was asked.
